checks.invariant: Failed logins for unknown, inactive, wrong-password and locked accounts are indistinguishable in body, status and timing (intent stated at backend/auth.py:64 and backend/app.py:450).
checks.result: Body and status are identical for every failure reason (backend/app.py:453). Unknown or inactive accounts run one bcrypt check against _DUMMY_HASH (backend/auth.py:104), which uses the same default cost as user hashes (backend/auth.py:53,66). The locked branch returns at backend/auth.py:107 without any bcrypt work, so response time reveals whether an account exists. Filed as candidate backend/auth.py:authenticate:locked-path-skips-bcrypt-timing; the timing gap still has to be measured locally.

checks.invariant: An Internet client cannot choose the address used for the per-IP login throttle or the IP recorded in sessions and audit_log.
checks.result: Behind Caddy (Caddyfile:2) the last X-Forwarded-For element is the one Caddy sets from its TCP peer, so the value is correct whether Caddy replaces or appends the header. However, client_ip trusts the header from any RFC1918, loopback or ULA peer (backend/auth.py:239-263). The backend is also published directly on 0.0.0.0:8000 (docker-compose.yml:10) and run with plain uvicorn (backend/Dockerfile:25). If Docker presents direct clients as a private gateway address, the client controls the header. Filed as candidate backend/auth.py:client_ip:xff-trusted-from-any-private-peer; a deployment fact decides it.

checks.invariant: Per-account lockout engages after MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS failures, refuses even correct passwords while locked, and updates its counter consistently.
checks.result: The UPDATE at backend/auth.py:112-121 evaluates both CASE expressions on the pre-update failed_attempts (PostgreSQL SET semantics), and RETURNING reports the new lock. A locked account is refused before password verification (backend/auth.py:106-107), and a successful login resets the counter (backend/auth.py:109-110). Anyone who knows an identifier can lock an account for LOCK_MINUTES. The login page announces this (backend/templates/login.html:248) and existing sessions stay valid, so it is a documented trade-off, recorded as hardening. Concurrent attempts read the lock before running bcrypt while holding a pooled connection (pool max 10, backend/db.py:25), so slightly more guesses than intended fit in one lock window; also recorded as hardening.

checks.invariant: bcrypt's 72-byte limit does not let a different password verify.
checks.result: hash_password (backend/auth.py:51-52) and password_issue (backend/auth.py:309-310), used by manage.py create-user and set-password (backend/manage.py:43,90,177), reject passwords over 72 bytes. verify_password truncates candidates to 72 bytes (backend/auth.py:58), so the only other input that verifies is a full 72-byte stored password with extra bytes appended. Password entropy is not reduced. No finding.

checks.invariant: Session identifiers are generated by the server, rotated on login, and cannot be fixed by an attacker.
checks.result: Each successful login issues a fresh secrets.token_urlsafe(32) token (backend/auth.py:140). Only its SHA-256 is stored (backend/auth.py:143-147; sessions.token_hash is UNIQUE in the schema), and the cookie is overwritten (backend/app.py:454-457). No path accepts a client-chosen value as a new session, so session fixation is not possible. A token already in the browser is not revoked on a new login; recorded as hardening.

checks.invariant: HTTP sessions stop working after logout, expiry, password reset and suspension.
checks.result: user_from_token requires revoked_at IS NULL, expires_at > now() and users.status = 'active' on every HTTP request (backend/auth.py:156-160). Logout revokes the row and deletes the cookie (backend/app.py:463-465). manage.py set-password and set-status revoke every session row for the user (backend/manage.py:178,189). The HTTP path is covered; the open-WebSocket gap is reported under the /ws/live unit.

checks.invariant: Cookie scope and transport do not let a less-trusted origin or network position obtain or replace the session cookie.
checks.result: The cookie is HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, host-only (no Domain), Path=/, with Max-Age equal to the server-side expiry (backend/auth.py:208-209). Secure is set when X-Forwarded-Proto is https (backend/auth.py:203-204). A client that spoofs that header only adds Secure and HSTS to its own response. On Caddy's TLS site the cookie is always Secure. No finding for this unit; plain-HTTP use of the direct port belongs to the deployment unit.

checks.invariant: A cross-site page cannot open /ws/live using the victim's cookie.
checks.result: origin_allowed (backend/auth.py:192-198) closes the socket with 4403 when the Origin host:port differs from Host, unless the origin is listed exactly in ALLOWED_ORIGINS (docker-compose.yml does not set it). Browsers always send Origin on WebSocket handshakes, so a request without Origin comes from a non-browser client that must already hold the cookie. The cookie is SameSite=Lax (backend/auth.py:209), which browsers withhold from cross-site WebSocket handshakes. The real client connects to location.host (backend/templates/index.html:733). Cross-site WebSocket hijacking is refuted; the scheme-blind comparison is recorded as hardening.

checks.invariant: At connect, the socket is bound to a valid, unrevoked, unexpired session of an active user.
checks.result: ws_live calls user_from_websocket (backend/app.py:546, then backend/auth.py:188-189 and the user_from_token checks at backend/auth.py:158-159) and closes with 4401 on failure before any frame is processed. accept() runs before these checks (backend/app.py:541), but no data is sent before the socket is closed.

checks.invariant: Logout, suspension, password reset and session expiry stop a live socket that is already open.
checks.result: The receive loop (backend/app.py:566-571) never re-checks the session token, account status, expiry or camera. manage.py set-status and set-password only update session rows (backend/manage.py:178,189), and logout only revokes the row (backend/app.py:463). Frames keep being analysed, MEDIO/ALTO results are inserted as events (backend/app.py:533; engine.py:146), and alerts are dispatched to the siren and Telegram (backend/app.py:534). Filed as candidate backend/app.py:ws_live:session-not-rechecked-after-accept; it needs local observation.

checks.invariant: A user can stream only into a camera they own.
checks.result: resolve_camera (backend/cameras.py:149-162) requires a UUID matching id, user_id equal to the session user, kind 'private' and is_active. An empty value selects or creates the user's own default camera (backend/cameras.py:128-146). Any other value closes the socket with 4404 (backend/app.py:558-560). The binding is captured once at connect, which is the same root cause as the stale-session candidate. No cross-user binding found.

checks.invariant: Socket responses disclose only data derived from the caller's own frames.
checks.result: Each response is the LiveSession.process result for the frame just received (engine.py:127-166, backend/app.py:569-571). No data from other users or cameras is read. No finding.

checks.invariant: Every cookie-authenticated unsafe route passes through the cross-site check.
checks.result: The unsafe routes are POST /login, /logout, /analyze, /ingest, /cameras and /cameras/{camera_id}/visibilidad (backend/app.py:437,461,576,618,706,737). The seguridad middleware (backend/app.py:488-497) wraps every HTTP request and returns 403 before routing when cross_site_request is true. /ingest authenticates only by bearer token (backend/app.py:621-625), so CSRF does not apply to it. There is no method override or alternate unsafe route.

checks.invariant: A cross-site browser request to an unsafe route is rejected.
checks.result: cross_site_request (backend/app.py:131-144) rejects any Origin whose host:port differs from Host and is not listed exactly in ALLOWED_ORIGINS; this includes 'null'. A malformed Origin makes urlparse raise, so the request fails closed. Without Origin, it rejects Sec-Fetch-Site values other than same-origin and none. It lets a request through only when both headers are absent, which current browsers never do for cross-origin POSTs. The check is effective for modern browsers. The pass-through when both headers are absent and the comparison that ignores the scheme are recorded as hardening.

checks.invariant: The session cookie is not attached to cross-site unsafe requests.
checks.result: vigia_session is set with an explicit SameSite=Lax (backend/auth.py:208-209), so browsers omit it on cross-site POST, fetch and subresource requests. Chrome's grace period that allows Lax cookies on POST applies only to cookies without a SameSite attribute. This is a second, independent layer.

GET routes only read data, except that they insert audit_log rows when an admin views another resident's camera or evidence (backend/app.py:675-682, 726-731), and only for resources the admin is authorised to see. A cross-site top-level navigation can trigger such a row. Low-impact hardening, not a finding.

checks.invariant: Login CSRF cannot sign a victim into an attacker's account.
checks.result: The login form (backend/templates/login.html:231) posts to POST /login, which needs no session cookie. Its only protection is the Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check, which rejects cross-site form posts from current browsers. Covered; the legacy-browser gap is recorded as hardening.

checks.invariant: A cross-site attacker cannot steer the Host value used as the comparison baseline.
checks.result: Caddy's reverse_proxy forwards the original Host (Caddyfile:1-2). An attacker cannot set the Host header of a victim's browser request, and a DNS-rebinding hostname would use a different cookie jar. No finding.

candidates.title: Locked-account login branch skips bcrypt, so response time reveals whether an account exists
candidates.description: POST /login is meant to make unknown, inactive, wrong-password and locked accounts indistinguishable: every failure returns the same 401 body, and unknown accounts run a dummy bcrypt check. The locked branch in auth.authenticate returns before any bcrypt work, while every other failure path runs exactly one bcrypt verification at the same default cost. An anonymous visitor can submit five wrong passwords for a candidate email or phone number and then time a sixth attempt. A registered account, now locked, answers without the bcrypt delay; an unregistered identifier answers after it. This reveals whether that email or phone belongs to a VIGIA resident or admin, and it locks the real account for LOCK_MINUTES as a side effect. The impact is limited to disclosure of account existence. The per-IP throttle (30 failures per 15 minutes) limits the rate to about five identifiers per source address per window.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: backend/auth.py authenticate returns 'locked' at the locked check before calling verify_password. The locked path therefore does no bcrypt work, while unknown, inactive and wrong-password paths each run one bcrypt verification at the same cost.

trace.description: Anonymous POST /login with form fields identifier and password.
Looks up the account by lower(email) or phone and computes the locked flag from locked_until.
Unknown or inactive identifier: one bcrypt verification against _DUMMY_HASH, then returns 'invalid'.
For an existing account, the fifth consecutive failure sets locked_until = now() + LOCK_MINUTES.
Locked account: returns 'locked' immediately with no bcrypt work, so the response comes back roughly one bcrypt duration sooner than for an unknown identifier.

evidence.description: Comment states the intent: the dummy hash makes a nonexistent user take the same time, so account existence cannot be deduced from response time.
Comment states the intent: the same message and code for 'does not exist', 'wrong password' and 'locked', so nobody can find out which accounts exist.
Identical 401 response for every failure reason; only timing differs.
Dummy hash is created with bcrypt.gensalt() at default cost.
User password hashes also use bcrypt.gensalt() at default cost, so unknown and wrong-password paths take the same time and only the locked path differs.
The per-IP throttle (defaults at backend/auth.py:34-35) limits the probe rate but does not remove the oracle.

blockers: No OS-enforced sandbox, PostgreSQL instance or bcrypt runtime was available and target code was not executed, so the response-time gap between the locked branch and the unknown-account branch has not been measured.

validation_plan.local: In a sandbox with a disposable local PostgreSQL loaded from bd_intivision/schema_vigia.sql and one dummy active user, call backend.auth.authenticate directly. Make five calls with a wrong password for the dummy user, then time a sixth call. Separately, time six calls for an unregistered identifier. The claim holds if the dummy user's sixth call returns 'locked' in milliseconds while the unregistered identifier's calls take about one bcrypt duration (hundreds of milliseconds at cost 12). Regression check: call verify_password(password, _DUMMY_HASH) before returning 'locked' and confirm the timings converge.

candidates.title: Open /ws/live sockets keep working after logout, suspension, password reset or session expiry
candidates.description: ws_live validates the vigia_session cookie once, right after the handshake, then loops indefinitely processing frames with the user and camera captured at connect time. HTTP routes re-check the session on every request (revoked_at, expires_at and users.status). backend/manage.py set-status and set-password explicitly revoke all sessions, so that a suspended or reset account 'loses its sessions'. Nothing closes or re-validates sockets that are already open. A resident who is suspended keeps a working socket, and so does someone using a stolen cookie whose sessions were revoked by a password reset. Each frame is still analysed. MEDIO/ALTO results are inserted as events attributed to that user and camera in the community's records. dispatch_live_alert still drives the shared MQTT siren and the Telegram channel. Socket lifetime is also not tied to the 12-hour session expiry.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: backend/app.py ws_live calls auth.user_from_websocket only once, before the receive loop. The loop over receive_bytes and _process_frame never re-checks the session token, account status, expiry or camera binding, and the server keeps no registry of open sockets to close when sessions are revoked.

trace.description: WebSocket /ws/live?camera= upgrade carrying the vigia_session cookie.
Session resolved once via auth.user_from_websocket; revocation, expiry and status are checked only at this moment.
Camera binding (owner, private, active) resolved once.
Receive loop accepts frames indefinitely with no session, status or expiry re-check.
Each frame is processed with the user and camera captured at connect time.
insert_event writes an event and evidence media row attributed to the captured user, community and camera.
dispatch_live_alert triggers the shared siren (ALTO) or warning (MEDIO) and sends a Telegram photo alert.

evidence.description: The HTTP session lookup requires revoked_at IS NULL, expires_at > now() and status 'active' on every request; the WebSocket path runs it only once.
set-status documents that a suspended account cannot log in and loses its sessions; line 189 only updates session rows.
set-password revokes all session rows to close open sessions; open sockets are unaffected.
Logout only revokes the session row; no socket is closed.
dispatch_live_alert triggers the siren for ALTO events, limited only by a global cooldown.
LiveSession.process emits an event for MEDIO/ALTO frames, so continued frames keep producing events and evidence.

blockers: Target code was not executed (no sandbox, PostgreSQL or YOLO models), so it was not observed that a socket opened before revocation keeps receiving, analysing and inserting frames after the session row is revoked or the user is suspended.
How long such a socket can stay open in deployment depends on uvicorn/websockets keepalive defaults and Caddy's WebSocket proxy timeouts. Source does not configure these and they were not observed.

validation_plan.local: In a sandbox with a disposable local PostgreSQL (schema_vigia.sql) and one dummy resident with a private camera, use Starlette TestClient against backend.app. Patch get_engine to return a stub whose session.process returns a fixed ALTO event, patch cv2.imdecode to return a small array, and patch get_dispatcher to a recording mock. Log in, open /ws/live?camera=<id> and send one frame. Then run UPDATE users SET status='suspended' and UPDATE sessions SET revoked_at=now(), as manage.py set-status does. Send a second frame on the same socket and count events rows and mock actuator.trigger calls. The claim holds if the second frame still inserts an event and calls the mock. Regression check: re-validate the token, status, expiry and camera per frame (or on a short interval) and close the socket with 4401.

candidates.title: client_ip trusts client-supplied X-Forwarded-For from any private or loopback peer, not only from Caddy
candidates.description: client_ip supplies the key for the per-IP login throttle and the address stored in sessions.ip and in the admin view_camera audit entry. It returns the last X-Forwarded-For element whenever the TCP peer is in 127/8, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, ::1 or fc00::/7. Through Caddy this is correct, because the last element is always the one Caddy sets from the real client. However, docker-compose.yml also publishes the backend directly on 0.0.0.0:8000. Docker may present an Internet client of that port as a private gateway address: for example, userland-proxy handling of IPv6 clients without ip6tables, rootless Docker, or Docker Desktop, or simply a client on the same private network. In that case the client's own X-Forwarded-For value is trusted. Each failed login can then claim a new address to escape the 30-failures-per-15-minutes throttle, leaving only the per-account lockout against password spraying. An attacker can also attribute failures to a victim's real address to block logins from it, and can forge the IP recorded in sessions and audit_log.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: backend/auth.py client_ip decides whether to trust the proxy header by membership in broad private ranges (_REDES_DE_CONFIANZA) instead of the specific Caddy proxy address. Any peer that appears private, including a direct client of the published port when Docker rewrites the source address, therefore supplies the address used by security controls.

trace.description: Anonymous POST /login with an arbitrary X-Forwarded-For header, reaching the backend directly on published port 8000.
The peer address is checked only for membership in the private and loopback ranges defined at backend/auth.py:239-240.
The last comma-separated X-Forwarded-For element is taken and returned if it parses as an IP address.
The per-IP throttle decision is keyed on the header-supplied address, and failures are recorded under it at backend/app.py:449.

evidence.description: Backend port 8000 is published on all host interfaces in addition to the Caddy ingress.
Caddy's reverse_proxy to backend:8000 is the only intended forwarding proxy.
Trusted networks are all RFC1918, loopback and ULA ranges rather than the proxy's address.
The throttle compares the failure count for the derived address against LOGIN_IP_MAX_FAILURES.
create_session stores the derived address in sessions.ip.
The admin view_camera audit entry records auth.client_ip(request).

blockers: Source does not show which address the backend container sees for an Internet client connecting directly to published port 8000; this is a Docker networking fact. With iptables DNAT the public address is preserved and the header is ignored. With userland-proxy handling (for example IPv6 clients without ip6tables), rootless Docker or Docker Desktop, the peer appears as a private gateway address and the header is trusted.
Whether port 8000 is reachable from the Internet at all (host or cloud firewall) is a deployment fact owned by the deployment unit and was not observed.
Target code was not executed, so the throttle bypass was not observed locally.

validation_plan.local: In a sandbox, build a Starlette Request whose scope client is ('172.18.0.1', 40000) with header X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7, and confirm that auth.client_ip returns '203.0.113.7'. Call register_failure 30 times for that address, then confirm throttled('203.0.113.7') is True and throttled('203.0.113.8') is False. Regression check: trust X-Forwarded-For only when the peer equals the configured Caddy address, or stop publishing port 8000.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner checks on the production host whether port 8000 is reachable externally and how Docker publishes it (docker info: rootless, userland-proxy, ip6tables). If it is reachable, the owner sends one failed dummy login from an external machine they control to http://<host>:8000/login with X-Forwarded-For: 198.51.100.1, then reads the backend log line 'Acceso fallido desde ...' to see which address was recorded.

hardening: Per-account lockout (backend/auth.py:112-121): anyone who knows a resident's email or phone can stop that account from starting new sessions by sending 5 failed logins every 15 minutes, which stays under the per-IP threshold. Existing sessions are unaffected and the behaviour is announced on the login page (backend/templates/login.html:248), so this is a documented design trade-off. Consider progressive delays, or lockout keyed on account plus source, instead of a hard account lock.

Lockout and throttle are check-then-act. backend/auth.py:96-107 reads the lock before bcrypt and the counter is updated only at backend/auth.py:112-121; backend/app.py:440 checks the per-IP count before backend/app.py:449 records the failure. Concurrent attempts, bounded by DB_POOL_MAX=10 (backend/db.py:25), allow up to about twice MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS guesses per lock window. Incrementing the counter atomically before verifying would close this.

cross_site_request (backend/app.py:143-144) lets unsafe requests through when they carry neither Origin nor Sec-Fetch-Site. Current browsers always send Origin on cross-origin POSTs and the cookie is explicitly SameSite=Lax, so only legacy browsers are exposed, including login CSRF on POST /login, which does not depend on a cookie. A per-form token, or rejecting unsafe requests that carry the cookie but no Origin, would remove the reliance on browser behaviour.

The Origin checks in cross_site_request (backend/app.py:142) and origin_allowed (backend/auth.py:198) compare only host:port with the Host header and ignore the scheme. A page served from http://intivision.online would pass; this requires an active network attacker before HSTS (backend/app.py:157-158) is cached. Compare the full scheme and host against the configured public origin.

GET /cameras/{id} (backend/app.py:726-731) and GET /evidence/{name} (backend/app.py:675-682) insert audit_log rows. SameSite=Lax sends the cookie on cross-site top-level navigations, so a third-party link can make an admin's browser record a view of a resource the admin is authorised to see.
The view_evidence audit row records request.client.host (backend/app.py:682), which behind Caddy is always the proxy container's address. view_camera uses client_ip instead (backend/app.py:731).

cookie_is_secure (backend/auth.py:203-204) trusts X-Forwarded-Proto from any peer, but spoofing it can only add Secure and HSTS to the requester's own response. Plain-HTTP logins on the directly published port 8000 send the password and a non-Secure session cookie in clear; port exposure itself is covered by the deployment unit.

A new login does not revoke a session token already present in the browser (backend/app.py:454-457), logout revokes only the current token (backend/app.py:463), and users have no way to revoke all their sessions.

ws_live calls accept() (backend/app.py:541) before the Origin and session checks. No data is exposed before the socket is closed, but rejecting before accept() would avoid allocating a connection for refused clients.

uncovered.boundary: PostgreSQL connection pool shared by all routes (backend/db.py ThreadedConnectionPool, DB_POOL_MAX default 10)
uncovered.attack_class: RESOURCE-EXHAUSTION-AND-AVAILABILITY: anonymous work holding a shared pooled connection
uncovered.reason: auth.authenticate keeps a pooled PostgreSQL connection checked out for the whole bcrypt verification (backend/auth.py:95-123), including the dummy check for unknown identifiers at line 104. The pool maximum is 10 (backend/db.py:25). Pool exhaustion raises psycopg2.pool.PoolError, which login_submit does not catch, so it is never registered as a failure by the per-IP throttle (backend/app.py:444-449). The open question is whether anonymous concurrent logins from several sources can make every DB-backed route and WebSocket authentication return 503. That is an availability boundary outside the assigned browser-session, CSRF and WebSocket-origin units, and outside the peer resource unit, which covers only /ingest and /analyze.
